passage:
Counselling note, Wednesday.
Jomon (second year, B.Com) came in with his friend Avni, who waited by the door. He had a slip from Saturday's campus health camp: one screening result for a rare blood condition marked "positive, repeat test advised". He had read that the screen is "95% accurate" and was convinced that meant he almost certainly had it. He said he hadn't slept much, and he kept rereading the slip. I did not interpret the result; that is not my role. Instead we wrote down his questions for the doctor, including "How many people who test positive on this screen actually turn out to have it?" He booked the repeat test before leaving. Avni offered to go with him. I will check in on Friday.

qa.q: What did Jomon's slip from the health camp say?
qa.a: One screening result for a rare blood condition was marked "positive, repeat test advised".

qa.q: Why does "95% accurate" make Jomon feel almost certain he is ill?
qa.a: Jomon feels frightened because "95% accurate" sounds to him like a 95% chance he has the condition, and the slip in his hand feels more real than the fact that the condition is rare to begin with.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help without giving medical advice?
qa.a: The counsellor helped Jomon write questions for the doctor, including how many positives turn out to be real, and he booked the repeat test.

qa.q: What might this week be like for Avni?
qa.a: Avni is probably worried and trying to stay steady for a friend, which is why Avni came along and offered to go to the test. 🤍

grounding: It shows a student reading a positive screen for a rare condition as near-certain illness without knowing how many positives are false.

Thursday, 11:40 p.m.
Can't sleep. The hostel screening report came today: "positive" for that rare kidney condition, the one with the long name. The sheet says the test catches it most of the time. So that's it, right? I've been searching symptoms online for three hours and I think I have half of them. My back does hurt sometimes.
Called Rashmi-di. She didn't panic, which was weirdly annoying. She asked how many people in a thousand even have this thing. I said I didn't know. She said, "Then you don't know yet what your positive means. Ask the doctor that exact question."
Appointment is Monday. Four days. I keep staring at the word POSITIVE in capitals.
- Jeevan

qa.a: Monday, four days away.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan feel so sure about having the condition?
qa.a: Jeevan feels panicked because the sheet says the test catches it most of the time and the capital-letter POSITIVE feels final, so Jeevan never thinks about how few people have the condition at all. 😰

qa.q: What would you advise Jeevan to do between now and Monday?
qa.a: Stop searching symptoms late at night, write down Rashmi-di's question about how many positives are real, and take it to the doctor on Monday.

qa.q: Why might Rashmi-di react so calmly?
qa.a: She seems to know that a positive for a rare condition can't be read without knowing how common it is, so she wants Jeevan to get that answer instead of spiralling.

grounding: It shows a student fearing a rare disease after a positive screen, without the context of how rare it is.

In the small town of Barpeta, the college health camp had set up tables in the library. Two days later the results came back, and Binita, nineteen, sat on the steps outside the pharmacy holding her slip. "Screening positive," it said, for a rare blood condition she had never heard of.
The leaflet said the test caught the condition in nearly everyone who had it. So I have it, she thought. Her hands went cold. She was already picturing telling Ma, missing her exams, the hospital in Guwahati.
Her cousin Divyansh sat down beside her and read the slip. "It says 'screening'. And 'confirmatory test advised'."
"But the test is nearly always right," Binita said. "That's what the leaflet says."
She folded the slip very small and didn't hear the rest.

qa.a: It said "Screening positive" for a rare blood condition she had never heard of.

qa.a: The leaflet says the test catches nearly everyone who has it, so a positive feels like proof; she doesn't stop to think how rare the condition is, which means many positives are false alarms.

qa.q: What choice could Binita make now instead of assuming the worst?
qa.a: She could take the slip back to the camp doctor and ask what a positive screening usually means for such a rare condition, and get the confirmatory test the slip advises.

It was past midnight in the student flats in Rotterdam, and Tuan had been reading about the rare nerve condition for three hours. The campus screening email sat open in the other tab: "Result: positive. Follow-up recommended."
"The test is ninety-nine percent accurate," he told Tomas, who had come out for water. "So it's ninety-nine percent that I've got it."
Tomas rubbed his eyes. "Is that what it means, though?"
"What else could it mean?" Tuan scrolled to photos of patients and felt sick. He started a draft email to his professor about dropping the June exams. He wrote a message to his mother in Da Nang and deleted it.
Tomas sat down. "Tomorrow, the student doctor opens at nine. Go and ask what the result actually means."
Tuan nodded, but kept scrolling.

qa.q: What did the campus screening email say?
qa.a: "Result: positive. Follow-up recommended."

qa.q: Why does Tuan believe it is ninety-nine percent that he has the condition?
qa.a: He confuses how accurate the test is with how likely he is to be ill, and forgets that when a condition is rare, a positive screening is often a false alarm.

qa.q: What is the wisest next step for Tuan, and why?
qa.a: Going to the student doctor at nine, as Tomas suggests, so a professional can explain what a positive result means for such a rare condition before he makes any decisions about his exams.

qa.q: If you were Tomas, finding a friend awake and frightened at midnight, what would you want?
qa.a: Tomas would want Tuan to stop reading scary pages and get real answers from a doctor, and probably to get some sleep before deciding anything.

passage: Swati, you asked why I went so quiet last month, so here it is. The college ran free health screenings, and a week later an email came: my result was 'positive, follow-up advised' for a rare blood condition. I read that line forty times. I'm Keerthana, I study statistics, and still I spent three nights reading every scary page online, deciding I had it. I even drafted a message to Amma in my head. Then the doctor at the follow-up drew a big box of dots on a notepad. She said the condition is so rare that most people who screen positive for it don't have it, which is why the proper test exists. That test came back clear. What stays with me is how certain I felt, holding one line of an email.

qa.a: The doctor's box of dots showed that most positives for a very rare condition are false alarms; next time Keerthana could ask the doctor what a positive means before searching online.

Monday. Lokesh gave blood at the campus camp and felt proud all day, the plaster on his arm like a badge.
Thursday. A letter came from the blood bank: one screening test on his sample had flagged, and he should see a doctor for a confirmatory test. He sat on his hostel bed reading about the rare liver condition named on the sheet, scrolling patient stories until 2 a.m. He texted his sister Uma: "I think I'm really sick." She called at once and stayed on the line until he fell asleep.
The next Tuesday. At the clinic, the doctor explained that blood-bank screens are set to catch everything, so for a rare condition most flags turn out to be false alarms; that is why the second test exists. The second test was clear. Walking out, Lokesh told Uma he would ask what a result means before he searched it next time.

passage: Ishita beta, sit with your Dadaji a minute, since you're worried about that report. In my second year at the engineering college in Pune, the college held an eye check. The nurse wrote on my card: 'suspected glaucoma, see specialist.' I, Madhav Joshi, a boy of nineteen, decided then and there I was going blind. I stopped reading at night, I wrote to my father that I might have to leave college. My friend Prakash, a quiet boy from Satara, dragged me to the library and found a book that said most young people flagged by that quick check are perfectly fine; the check catches many so it misses none. The specialist tested me properly and smiled kindly. Sixty years I have read since then. So first, we ask the doctor what your number means.

passage: In their Pune flat, Payal stared at the report from the company health check. One line was flagged in red: a screening test for a rare liver condition, "reactive." She stopped eating. She told her sister Tanuja she was sure she had it. "The report says so." Tanuja, who worked at a diagnostic lab, sat down with her. "Payal, how rare is this condition?" "Very rare. It says so here." "Right. So when thousands of healthy people take a screening test, a few will show up reactive even though they're fine. For something this rare, those false alarms can be more than the real cases." Payal blinked. "So I probably don't have it?" "Probably not. But we don't guess. The doctor will order the proper test." Payal went to the doctor the next morning. The second test was normal. She cried with relief in the car.

qa.q: What was flagged in red on Payal's report?
qa.a: A screening test for a rare liver condition, "reactive."

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she stopped eating?
qa.a: She felt frightened and certain she had the rare condition because the report seemed to say so.

qa.q: How did Tanuja help Payal, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She explained that false alarms can outnumber real cases for rare conditions, and still insisted on seeing the doctor for the proper test.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel watching her sister's fear?
qa.a: Tanuja probably felt concerned but steady, using her lab knowledge to calm Payal without dismissing her.

grounding: Shows a young adult sure she has a rare condition after a positive screening, until her sister explains false alarms and a doctor checks.

Last month the college health camp ran a free screening, and my result came back flagged: "positive, further testing advised" for a rare blood condition I'd never heard of. I'm Francis, and I spent the next four nights reading about it until 3 a.m.
The leaflet called the test highly accurate. In my head that meant: accurate test, positive result, so I have it. I wrote a list of people to tell. I stopped eating properly.
My roommate Joseph dragged me to the campus doctor on Monday. She drew a grid on a notepad and explained that the condition is so rare that, even with a good test, most people who screen positive turn out not to have it. That's why there's a second test.
The second test was clear.
What stays with me is how certain I felt. The word "accurate" was so loud that I never asked how rare the thing was to begin with.

qa.q: What did the flagged result say?
qa.a: It said 'positive, further testing advised' for a rare blood condition.

qa.q: Why was Francis so sure of having the condition?
qa.a: Francis felt terrified, and the word 'accurate' made a positive result feel certain, without any thought about how rare the condition was.

qa.q: What helped Francis, and what could Francis do differently next time?
qa.a: Seeing the campus doctor helped; next time Francis could ask a doctor to explain a result straight away instead of reading alone until 3 a.m.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt during those four nights?
qa.a: Joseph was likely worried and helpless watching Francis stop eating, which is why Joseph dragged Francis to the doctor.

passage:
Counselling note, student wellness centre. Written by Anand, counsellor.
Jaya, a first-year, came in today shaking, holding a printout from last week's campus health screening. One line was marked "reactive", for a rare condition. She had already searched online and told me, "The test is ninety-something percent accurate, so I'm ninety-something percent sick."
I listened first. She had not slept properly for three nights and had missed two classes.
I did not interpret the result; that is the doctor's job. I said that screening results for rare conditions often need a second test, and that only a doctor could explain what hers meant.
What I did next: I phoned the campus clinic while she sat with me and got her a slot that afternoon. I asked her to write down her questions, starting with: how common is this, and what does a positive screen usually mean? She left calmer, list in hand.

qa.q: What was the line on Jaya's printout marked?
qa.a: One line was marked 'reactive', for a rare condition.

qa.q: Why did Jaya believe she was 'ninety-something percent sick'?
qa.a: Jaya was frightened and took the test's accuracy as her chance of being ill, without weighing how rare the condition is.

qa.q: Why was booking the clinic slot and a question list a good step?
qa.a: It got Jaya to a doctor the same afternoon to explain the result, with a first question about how common the condition is.

qa.q: How did the session look to Anand?
qa.a: Anand saw a frightened, sleepless student and chose to listen, avoid interpreting the result, and get her to the doctor quickly.

grounding: Shows a student who fears a rare disease after a positive screen, seen through a counsellor's note, and is sent to a doctor for context.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m.
The job medical today flagged my eye test. "Possible early sign of a rare eye condition. Refer to specialist." I read that line about forty times on the bus.
By dinner I had decided I was going blind. The machine is modern. Machines don't lie. I even looked up braille classes.
Deepak found me crying on the balcony. He's studying statistics, so he drew dots on the back of an envelope: thousands of people, a tiny cluster who actually have it, and a bigger group of healthy people the machine flags by mistake. "If it's rare, most flags are false alarms," he said. "Not all. Most. That's why they send you to a specialist."
I'm still scared. But I'm less sure I'm doomed.
The appointment is Friday. Deepak's coming. I'm writing my questions now.
Trisha

qa.a: It flagged Trisha's eye test as a possible early sign of a rare eye condition.

qa.a: Trisha was frightened and convinced of going blind, trusting the modern machine without thinking about how rare the condition is.
